questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A boy, standing at a certain height, kicks a football horizontally with a velocity of $19.6\ ms^{-1}$. What will be the ratio of horizontal and vertical components of velocities after 2s?
questions.solution:
Initial horizontal velocity, $u_x = 19.6\ ms^{-1}$

Initial vertical velocity, $u_y = 0\ ms^{-1}$

Acceleration in horizontal direction, $a_x = 0$

Acceleration in vertical direction, $a_y = g = 9.8\ ms^{-2}$

Time, $t = 2\ s$

Horizontal velocity after $2\ s$, $v_x = u_x + a_x t = 19.6\ ms^{-1}$

Vertical velocity after $2\ s$, $v_y = u_y + a_y t = 0 + 9.8 \times 2 = 19.6\ ms^{-1}$

Ratio of horizontal and vertical components of velocities $= \dfrac{v_x}{v_y} = \dfrac{19.6}{19.6} = 1:1$

Answer: $1:1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: From the same point, two stones A and B are thrown simultaneously, A is thrown up vertically with a velocity of $10\ ms^{-1}$ and B is thrown up with the same velocity at $30^{}^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. The separation between the balls at 2 s is
questions.solution:
Let the point of projection be the origin $(0,0)$.

Position vector of stone A at time $t$ is:

$\vec{r}_A = (10t - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2)\hat{j}$

Position vector of stone B at time $t$ is:

$\vec{r}_B = (10\cos 30^{}^{\circ} t)\hat{i} + (10\sin 30^{}^{\circ} t - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2)\hat{j}$

$\vec{r}_B = 5\sqrt{3}t\hat{i} + (5t - \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2)\hat{j}$

The relative position vector of A with respect to B is:

$\vec{r}_{AB} = \vec{r}_A - \vec{r}_B = -5\sqrt{3}t\hat{i} + 5t\hat{j}$

The separation between the stones is the magnitude of $\vec{r}_{AB}$:

$|\vec{r}_{AB}| = \sqrt{(-5\sqrt{3}t)^2 + (5t)^2}$

$|\vec{r}_{AB}| = \sqrt{75t^2 + 25t^2} = \sqrt{100t^2} = 10t$

At $t = 2\text{ s}$, the separation is:

$d = 10 \times 2 = 20\text{ m}$

Answer: $20\ \text{m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: For a projectile, the square of its horizontal range is equal to 8 times the square of the maximum height it reached. What is the angle of projection of the projectile?
questions.solution:
The horizontal range $R$ of a projectile is given by $R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g} = \dfrac{2u^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta}{g}$.

The maximum height $H$ of a projectile is given by $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$.

The problem states that $R^2 = 8H^2$. Substituting the expressions for $R$ and $H$:

$\left( \dfrac{2u^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta}{g} \right)^2 = 8 \left( \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g} \right)^2$

$\dfrac{4u^4 \sin^2\theta \cos^2\theta}{g^2} = 8 \left( \dfrac{u^4 \sin^4\theta}{4g^2} \right)$

$\dfrac{4u^4 \sin^2\theta \cos^2\theta}{g^2} = \dfrac{2u^4 \sin^4\theta}{g^2}$

Dividing both sides by $\dfrac{2u^4 \sin^2\theta}{g^2}$ (assuming $\sin\theta \neq 0$):

$2 \cos^2\theta = \sin^2\theta$

$\tan^2\theta = 2$

$\tan\theta = \sqrt{2}$

$\theta = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{2})$

Answer: $\theta=\tan ^{-1}(\sqrt{2})$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Rain is falling vertically downwards at a velocity $9 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$. And wind starts blowing at a speed of $4 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ in the west to east direction. In which direction should the girl hold her umbrella to protect herself from the rain?
questions.solution:
Let the velocity of rain be $\vec{v}_{r} = -9 \hat{j} \text{ ms}^{-1}$, where $\hat{j}$ is the unit vector in the upward vertical direction.

The velocity of the wind is $\vec{v}_{w} = 4 \hat{i} \text{ ms}^{-1}$, where $\hat{i}$ is the unit vector in the west to east direction.

The velocity of the rain with respect to the girl (who is assumed to be stationary) is $\vec{v}_{rg} = \vec{v}_{r} - \vec{v}_{w} = -4 \hat{i} - 9 \hat{j} \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

To protect herself from the rain, the girl must hold the umbrella in the direction of the relative velocity of the rain, which is $\vec{v}_{rg} = -4 \hat{i} - 9 \hat{j}$.

The angle $\theta$ that the umbrella makes with the vertical is given by $\tan \theta = \dfrac{|v_{x}|}{|v_{y}|} = \dfrac{4}{9}$.

Calculating the value, $\tan \theta = 0.444... \approx 0.44$.

Since the horizontal component of the relative velocity is $-4 \hat{i}$ (directed towards the west), the girl must tilt the umbrella towards the west to counter the rain coming from the east.

Answer: $\theta=\tan ^{-1}(0.44)$ with the vertical towards west

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gun is used to fire a bullet at an angle of $30^{{}^{\circ}}$ and at $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ respectively. The ratios of heights and Ranges reached by the bullet are
questions.solution:
Maximum height: $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$

$H_1 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 30°}{2g} = \dfrac{u^2}{8g}$, $\quad H_2 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 60°}{2g} = \dfrac{3u^2}{8g}$

$H_1 : H_2 = 1 : 3$

Range: $R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g}$

$R_1 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin 60°}{g}$, $\quad R_2 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin 120°}{g}$

Since $\sin 60° = \sin 120°$, $R_1 = R_2 \Rightarrow R_1 : R_2 = 1 : 1$

Ratio of heights : ranges $= 1:3,\ 1:1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A boy is running along a straight horizontal road with a constant speed $5 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$. While running he throws a stone with a velocity $30 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ at an angle $60^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the horizontal. Then the time of flight of the stone is: (Given $g=10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ )
questions.solution:
The velocity of the stone is given with respect to the boy. Let the velocity of the boy be $\vec{v}_b = 5 \hat{i} \text{ ms}^{-1}$. The velocity of the stone with respect to the boy is $\vec{v}_{s/b} = 30 \cos 60^{{}^{\circ}} \hat{i} + 30 \sin 60^{{}^{\circ}} \hat{j} \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

The velocity of the stone with respect to the ground is $\vec{v}_s = \vec{v}_{s/b} + \vec{v}_b = (30 \times 0.5 + 5) \hat{i} + (30 \times \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \hat{j} \text{ ms}^{-1} = 20 \hat{i} + 15\sqrt{3} \hat{j} \text{ ms}^{-1}$.

The time of flight $T$ for a projectile depends only on the vertical component of the initial velocity $u_y$ and the acceleration due to gravity $g$.

$T = \dfrac{2 u_y}{g} = \dfrac{2 \times 15\sqrt{3}}{10} = \dfrac{30\sqrt{3}}{10} = 3\sqrt{3} \text{ s}$.

Answer: $3 \sqrt{3}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three identical conducting balls A, B and C, each of mass m, are thrown upward at an angle $\Theta$ to the horizontal with an initial speed $v$ in a region of space that has a uniform electric field $E$ downward along with the gravitational field $g$. A is positively charged, B is uncharged and C is negatively charged. Rank the ranges R of these three balls in increasing order.
questions.solution:
The range $R$ of a projectile launched with initial speed $v$ at an angle $\Theta$ is given by $R = \dfrac{v^2 \sin(2\Theta)}{g_{eff}}$, where $g_{eff}$ is the effective acceleration acting on the particle in the downward direction.

For ball B (uncharged), the only force acting is gravity, so $g_{eff, B} = g$.

For ball A (positively charged), the electric force $qE$ acts in the same direction as gravity (downward), so the effective acceleration is $g_{eff, A} = g + \dfrac{qE}{m}$. Since $g_{eff, A} > g$, the range $R_A$ is smaller than $R_B$.

For ball C (negatively charged), the electric force $qE$ acts in the opposite direction to gravity (upward), so the effective acceleration is $g_{eff, C} = g - \dfrac{qE}{m}$. Since $g_{eff, C} < g$, the range $R_C$ is larger than $R_B$.

Comparing the effective accelerations, $g_{eff, A} > g_{eff, B} > g_{eff, C}$.

Since the range is inversely proportional to the effective acceleration, we have $R_A < R_B < R_C$.

Answer: $R_A < R_B < R_C$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A piece of marble is projected from Earth's surface with velocity of $19.6 \sqrt{2} \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ at $45^{{}^{\circ}}$. After 2 s , its velocity makes an angle $\alpha$ with horizontal, where $\alpha$ is
questions.solution: $u_x=19.6 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ and $u_y=19.6 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$. After 2 s , vertical component of velocity $v_y$ will become zero. So, particle is at its highest point.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two balls are thrown horizontally, one from the window of first floor which is $3 \mathrm{ m}$ high from the ground and second from the second floor which is $6 \mathrm{ m}$ high from the ground, of a multi storey building, with the same speed of $6 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$. Calculate the distance that will separate the two balls when they hit the ground.
questions.solution:
The time taken for a ball thrown horizontally from a height $h$ to reach the ground is given by $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

For the first ball thrown from height $h_1 = 3$ m:
$t_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 3}{9.8}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{6}{9.8}} \approx 0.7825$ s.

The horizontal distance covered by the first ball is $x_1 = v \times t_1 = 6 \times 0.7825 = 4.695$ m.

For the second ball thrown from height $h_2 = 6$ m:
$t_2 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 6}{9.8}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{12}{9.8}} \approx 1.1066$ s.

The horizontal distance covered by the second ball is $x_2 = v \times t_2 = 6 \times 1.1066 = 6.6396$ m.

The distance separating the two balls when they hit the ground is the difference in their horizontal ranges:
$\Delta x = x_2 - x_1 = 6.6396 - 4.695 = 1.9446$ m.

Rounding to two decimal places, the distance is $1.94$ m.

Answer: 1.94 m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A cricketer of height $2.5 \mathrm{ m}$ throws a ball at an angle of $30^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the horizontal such that it is received by another cricketer of same height standing at a distance of $50 \mathrm{ m}$ from the first one. The maximum height attained by the ball is (\tan 30^{{}^{\circ}}=0.577$)$
questions.solution:
The height of both cricketers is $h = 2.5 \text{ m}$. Since the ball is thrown and received at the same height, the vertical displacement is zero. The horizontal range $R$ is given by $R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}$.

Given $R = 50 \text{ m}$ and $\theta = 30^{{}^{\circ}}$, we have $50 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(60^{{}^{\circ}})}{g} = \dfrac{u^2 \sqrt{3}}{2g}$.

Thus, $\dfrac{u^2}{g} = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{3}}$.

The maximum height $H$ attained by the projectile above the point of projection is given by $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$.

Substituting the value of $\dfrac{u^2}{g}$:

$H = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \left( \dfrac{u^2}{g} \right) \times \sin^2(30^{{}^{\circ}}) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{3}} \times \left( \dfrac{1}{2} \right)^2 = \dfrac{100}{8\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{12.5}{1.732} \approx 7.216 \text{ m}$.

The total maximum height from the ground is $H_{total} = h + H = 2.5 + 7.216 = 9.716 \text{ m}$.

Rounding to the nearest value provided in the options, we get $9.7 \text{ m}$.

Answer: 9.7 m

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball is moving in a circular path of radius $5 \mathrm{ m}$. If tangential acceleration at any instant is $10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ and the net acceleration makes an angle of $30^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the centripetal acceleration, then, the instantaneous speed is
questions.solution:
The tangential acceleration is given as $a_t = 10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$.

The centripetal acceleration is given by $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r}$, where $v$ is the instantaneous speed and $r = 5 \mathrm{ m}$. Thus, $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{5}$.

The net acceleration $\vec{a}$ is the vector sum of the tangential acceleration $\vec{a}_t$ and the centripetal acceleration $\vec{a}_c$. Since $\vec{a}_t$ and $\vec{a}_c$ are perpendicular, the angle $\theta$ between the net acceleration $\vec{a}$ and the centripetal acceleration $\vec{a}_c$ is given by $\tan \theta = \dfrac{a_t}{a_c}$.

Given $\theta = 30^{{}^{\circ}}$, we have $\tan 30^{{}^{\circ}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.

Substituting the values, $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{10}{v^2 / 5} = \dfrac{50}{v^2}$.

Therefore, $v^2 = 50 \sqrt{3}$.

Calculating the value, $v^2 = 50 \times 1.732 = 86.6$.

$v = \sqrt{86.6} \approx 9.3 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$.

Answer: $9.3 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is moving along a circular path of radius '$r$' with a frequency of revolution numerically equal to the radius of the circular path. What is the acceleration of the body if radius of the path is $\left(\dfrac{5}{\pi}\right) m$ ?
questions.solution:
The acceleration of a body moving in a circular path is the centripetal acceleration, given by $a = \omega^2 r$.

The angular velocity $\omega$ is related to the frequency $f$ by the formula $\omega = 2 \pi f$.

Given that the frequency $f$ is numerically equal to the radius $r$, we have $f = r$.

Substituting $f = r$ into the expression for $\omega$, we get $\omega = 2 \pi r$.

The acceleration $a$ becomes $a = (2 \pi r)^2 r = 4 \pi^2 r^3$.

Given the radius $r = \dfrac{5}{\pi}$ m, we substitute this value into the expression for $a$:

$a = 4 \pi^2 \left(\dfrac{5}{\pi}\right)^3

a = 4 \pi^2 \left(\dfrac{125}{\pi^3}\right)

$a = $\dfrac{4 \times 125}{\pi} = \dfrac{500}{\pi}\text{ ms}^{-2}$.

Answer: $\left(\dfrac{500}{\pi}\right) \mathrm{ms}^{-2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal ball of $20 \mathrm{ g}$ is projected at an angle $30^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the horizontal with an initial velocity $10 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$. If the mass and angle of projection are doubled keeping the initial velocity the same, the ratio of the maximum height attained in the former to the latter case is :
questions.solution:
The maximum height $H$ attained by a projectile is given by the formula $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$, where $u$ is the initial velocity, $\theta$ is the angle of projection, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

In the first case, $u_1 = 10 \text{ ms}^{-1}$ and $\theta_1 = 30^{{}^{\circ}}$. The maximum height is $H_1 = \dfrac{u_1^2 \sin^2(30^{{}^{\circ}})}{2g} = \dfrac{10^2 \times (1/2)^2}{2g} = \dfrac{100 \times 1/4}{2g} = \dfrac{25}{2g}$.

In the second case, the mass is doubled (which does not affect the height), the velocity remains $u_2 = 10 \text{ ms}^{-1}$, and the angle is doubled, so $\theta_2 = 2 \times 30^{{}^{\circ}} = 60^{{}^{\circ}}$. The maximum height is $H_2 = \dfrac{u_2^2 \sin^2(60^{{}^{\circ}})}{2g} = \dfrac{10^2 \times (\sqrt{3}/2)^2}{2g} = \dfrac{100 \times 3/4}{2g} = \dfrac{75}{2g}$.

The ratio of the maximum height in the former case to the latter case is $\dfrac{H_1}{H_2} = \dfrac{25/2g}{75/2g} = \dfrac{25}{75} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

Answer: 1 : 3

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One end of the string of length $l$ is connected to a particle of mass $m$ and the other end is connected to a small peg on a smooth horizontal table. If the particle moves in circle with speed $v$, the net force on the particle (directed towards centre) will be (T$ represents the tension in the string)$
questions.solution:
Consider the string of length $l$ connected to a particle as shown in the figure

Speed of the particle is $v$. As, the particle is in uniform circular motion, the net force on the particle must be equal to centripetal force which is provided by the tension $(T)$.
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \text{ Net force } & =\text{ Centripetal force } \\
& =\text{ Tension$ in $string } \\
\Rightarrow \quad \frac{m v^2}{l} & =T
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hockey player hits the ball at an angle of $37^{{}^{\circ}}$ from the horizontal with an initial speed of $40 \mathrm{ m} / \mathrm{s}$ (a right angled triangle with one of the angle is $37^{{}^{\circ}}$ and their sides in the ratio of $6: 8: 10$). Assume that the ball is in a vertical plane. The time at which the ball reaches the highest point of its path is
questions.solution:
The initial velocity of the ball is $u = 40 \text{ m/s}$ and the angle of projection is $\theta = 37^{{}^{\circ}}$.

The vertical component of the initial velocity is given by $u_y = u \sin \theta$.

Given the triangle with sides in ratio $3:4:5$ (which is equivalent to $6:8:10$), $\sin 37^{{}^{\circ}} = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

Substituting the values, $u_y = 40 \times \dfrac{3}{5} = 8 \times 3 = 24 \text{ m/s}$.

At the highest point of the trajectory, the vertical component of the velocity becomes zero, $v_y = 0$.

Using the equation of motion $v_y = u_y - gt$, where $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$ is the acceleration due to gravity:

$0 = 24 - 10t$

$10t = 24$

$t = 2.4 \text{ s}$.

Answer: 2.4 s

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball is projected horizontally with a velocity of $5 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ from the top of a building $19.6 \mathrm{ m}$ high. How long will the ball take to hit the ground?
questions.solution:
The motion of the ball in the vertical direction is governed by the equation of motion under constant acceleration due to gravity $g = 9.8 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$.

The vertical displacement $h$ is given by $h = u_y t + \dfrac{1}{2} g t^2$, where $u_y$ is the initial vertical velocity.

Since the ball is projected horizontally, the initial vertical velocity $u_y = 0$.

Substituting the given values $h = 19.6 \mathrm{ m}$ and $g = 9.8 \mathrm{ ms}^{-2}$ into the equation:

$19.6 = 0 \times t + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 9.8 \times t^2$

$19.6 = 4.9 t^2$

$t^2 = \dfrac{19.6}{4.9}$

$t^2 = 4$

$t = 2 \mathrm{ s}$

Answer: $2 \mathrm{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two guns $P$ and $Q$ can fire bullets at speeds $2 \mathrm{ km} / \mathrm{s}$ and $4 \mathrm{ km} / \mathrm{s}$, respectively. From a point on a horizontal ground, they are fired in all possible directions. The ratio of maximum or areas covered by the bullets fired by the two guns, on the ground is
questions.solution:
The maximum horizontal range $R$ of a projectile fired with speed $v$ is given by the formula $R = \dfrac{v^2}{g}$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

The bullets are fired in all possible directions, so the area covered on the ground is a circle with radius $R$. The area $A$ is given by $A = \pi R^2 = \pi \left( \dfrac{v^2}{g} \right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi v^4}{g^2}$.

For gun $P$, the speed is $v_P = 2 \text{ km/s}$. The area covered is $A_P = \dfrac{\pi (2)^4}{g^2} = \dfrac{16\pi}{g^2}$.

For gun $Q$, the speed is $v_Q = 4 \text{ km/s}$. The area covered is $A_Q = \dfrac{\pi (4)^4}{g^2} = \dfrac{256\pi}{g^2}$.

The ratio of the areas covered is $\dfrac{A_P}{A_Q} = \dfrac{16\pi / g^2}{256\pi / g^2} = \dfrac{16}{256} = \dfrac{1}{16}$.

Answer: $1: 16$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The angle of projection with the horizontal in terms of maximum height attained and horizontal range is given by
questions.solution:
The maximum height $H$ attained by a projectile is given by $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$.

The horizontal range $R$ of the projectile is given by $R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g} = \dfrac{2u^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta}{g}$.

Dividing the expression for $H$ by the expression for $R$, we get:

$\dfrac{H}{R} = \dfrac{\dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}}{\dfrac{2u^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta}{g}}$

$\dfrac{H}{R} = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g} \times \dfrac{g}{2u^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta}$

$\dfrac{H}{R} = \dfrac{\sin \theta}{4 \cos \theta} = \dfrac{1}{4} \tan \theta$

Rearranging the terms to solve for $\tan \theta$:

$\tan \theta = \dfrac{4H}{R}$

Therefore, the angle of projection $\theta$ is given by:

$\theta = \tan^{-1} \left(\dfrac{4H}{R}\right)

Answer: $\tan ^{-1} $\left(\dfrac{4 H}{R}\right)$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body is projected vertically upwards. The times corresponding to height $h$, while ascending and while descending are $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$, respectively. Then, the velocity of projection is (g$ is acceleration due to gravity)$
questions.solution:
Let $u$ be the initial velocity of vertical projection and $t$ be the time taken by the body to reach at height $h$ from the ground.
$\therefore$ Using equation, $h=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$
Here, $u=u, a=-g\therefore \quad h=u t-\frac{1}{2} g t^{2}\Rightarrow \quad g t^{2}-2 u t+2 h=0\therefore \quad t=\frac{2 u \pm \sqrt{4 u^{2}-4 g \times 2 h}}{2 g}=\frac{u \pm \sqrt{u^{2}-2 g h}}{g}$
It means $t$ has two values, $t_{1} and t_{2}$. Where, $t_{1}$ is time taken by the body in reaching maximum height and $t_{2}$ be the time taken by the body in reaching ground from maximum height. $\begin{aligned}&\therefore \quad t_{1}=\frac{u+\sqrt{u^{2}-2 g h}}{g}\\
&\text{ and } \quad t_{2}=\frac{u-\sqrt{u^{2}-2 g h}}{g}\\
&\therefore \quad t_{1}+t_{2}=\frac{2 u}{g} \text{ or } u=\frac{g\left(t_{1}+t_{2}\right)}{2}
\end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: From the top of a tower, two stones whose masses are in the ratio $1: 2$ are thrown-one straight up with an initial speed $u$ and the second straight down with the same speed $u$. Then, neglecting air resistance
options: the heavier stone hits the ground with a higher speed
the lighter stone hits the ground with a higher speed
Both the stones will have the same speed when they hit the ground
the speed can't be determined with the given data
questions.solution:
The first stone move up to some height and then its velocity becomes zero. Now, it move downward and at the level of top of tower, it acquires the same initial velocity $u$ and gravitational acceleration $g$ in downward direction.
The second stone is moving with the same speed $u$ and with downward acceleration $g$. So, both will have same final velocity when they reach the bottom and hit the ground.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is moving eastward with a velocity $5 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$. In $10 \mathrm{ s}$ the velocity changes to $5 \mathrm{ ms}^{-1}$ northwards. The average acceleration in this time is
questions.solution:
Given, $u=5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$, Eastwards 
$v=5 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$, Northwards
and $\Delta t=10 \mathrm{~s}$
Change in velocity $|\Delta v|=\sqrt{u^{2}+v^{2}}$
=$\sqrt{5^{2}+5^{2}}=$5 $\sqrt{2} \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$Direction of $\Delta v$,

\tan $\theta=\frac{v}{u}=\frac{-5}{5}=-$1

(taking eastward direction positive)

\Rightarrow \quad $\theta=$135^{{}^{\circ}}

$\therefore$ Average acceleration, 
$a_{\text{avg }}=\frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}=\frac{5 \sqrt{2}}{10}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$, towards North-West

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is projected at an angle of $30^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the horizontal with a momentum $p$. At the highest point its momentum is
questions.solution:
Let $m$ be the mass of particle and $u$ be its initial velocity, then Initial momentum, $p=m u \quad \text{...(i)}$ At highest point,

$\begin{aligned} v_{x} &=u \cos \theta=u \cos 30^{{}^{\circ}} \\ &=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} u \\ v_{y} &=0 \end{aligned}\therefore$ Momentum at highest point is $\begin{array}{rlr}p^{\prime}=m v_{x} & =m u\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) & \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} p \quad \text{ [using Eq. (i)] }\end{array}$
